title: A Gmail deliverability guide: Getting and staying in good standing
summary: Succeeding with Gmail deliverability comes down to trust. Senders who meet the technical requirements, authenticate properly, honor unsubscribe requests, and keep complaints low, clear the baseline. But lasting inbox placement depends on something deeper: consistently sending mail that subscribers actually want, at a pace and cadence they can predict. Senders who respect their audience, stay vigilant about engagement signals, and adapt as Google's tools and requirements evolve will be the ones who maintain strong standing over time.
body_markdown:
***TL;DR***


*Succeeding with Gmail deliverability comes down to trust. Senders who meet the technical requirements, authenticate properly, honor unsubscribe requests, and keep complaints low, clear the baseline. But lasting inbox placement depends on something deeper: consistently sending mail that subscribers actually want, at a pace and cadence they can predict. Senders who respect their audience, stay vigilant about engagement signals, and adapt as Google's tools and requirements evolve will be the ones who maintain strong standing over time.*


***Key takeaways***


- ***Reputation is earned through recipient behavior, not sender intent.** Google bases placement decisions on how subscribers actually respond to mail, not on what the sender hopes to achieve.*
- ***Authentication is the price of entry.** SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are now baseline requirements for bulk senders, not optional best practices.*
- ***Complaint rates have hard limits.** Senders must stay below 0.1% and never exceed 0.3%, with one click unsubscribe now a requirement for marketing mail.*
- ***Warming and consistency protect long-term standing.** A slow, deliberate ramp into Google's ecosystem and a steady, predictable send cadence both reduce the risk of reputation damage.*
- ***Postmaster Tools remains essential, even as it evolves.** GPMT v2 removes the simple reputation labels senders relied on, so monitoring engagement signals directly becomes more important going forward.*
- ***Email doesn't operate alone.** Complementary channels like SMS, push, and social can draw attention back to email and help improve how providers view engagement with a sender's messages.*


When it comes to inbox providers, Gmail is consistently near the top—chosen by a plurality of email recipients in the US and around the world. Accordingly, maintaining a strong sender reputation with Google is one of the most important things that an email marketer can do. Keep that relationship strong, and you can support the successful delivery of messages to your audience of Gmail users; neglect it and run the risk of seeing your messages filtered out of your users' inboxes.


For many senders, maintaining a strong reputation requires not just a logistical change, but also sometimes culture or behavioral changes as well. Google is very focused on protecting its users from unwanted commercial emails (i.e. spam) and its filtering approach is centered on how recipients interact with what senders share with them. That means that the biggest factor in determining your sender reputation with Gmail is how the people receiving your emails are engaging with them. If they're acting in ways that indicate the mail is desired, you're on the right track—and if they aren't, you're likely going to face challenges.


## **Google's approach to engagement**


Google's email placement decisions are heavily based on sender reputation—and that reputation is based on the engagement signals that subscribers send. Here are a few key engagement signals that can impact your reputation when sending to Google (as well as to other inbox providers):


- **Positive Signals:** Opening an email, clicking links, marking a message as "not spam," and adding the sender’s address to a contact list.
- **Negative Signals:** Deleting a piece of mail without opening it, marking it as spam, or simply ignoring it.
- **Indiscriminate Sending:** Sending to non-existent users or typo domains (like "[gnail.com](http://gnail.com/) "), which may or may not be monitored, is seen as a sign of poor list hygiene and can negatively impact reputation.


## **Listening to the signals: Google Postmaster Tools**


[Google Postmaster Tools (GPMT) version 1](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/google-postmaster-tools-v1-interface-retirement) provides visibility into how Google views your domain and IP reputation. The dashboard typically requires a specific volume threshold to operate effectively—recently, their Bulk Sender guidelines have recommended an entry point of 500 recipients, and data usually isn’t displayed below that level.


### **Reputation Levels (and what they look like)**


- **High:** Your mail has a very low spam rate and complies with Google’s sender guidelines. Mail will rarely be filtered by the spam filter, but may still be placed there under some circumstances via individual user settings.
- **Medium:** Most mail is delivered to the inbox, but some might be filtered if the spam rate increases.
- **Low:** Your mail is frequently filtered as spam. This indicates that Google sees more negative user feedback than positive engagement.
- **Bad:** A high history of spam. Mail from this sender will almost always be filtered or rejected.


Google is in the process of sunsetting GMPT version 1 and replacing it with version 2. One side effect of this change is that marketers will not be able to see IP/domain reputation ratings in the new dashboard, potentially making it a bit more challenging to understand that aspect of their deliverability efforts. Once the v1 dashboard is deprecated, senders will have to rely more on the response signals from the recipients, requiring increased vigilance in connection with KPI fluctuations that could signal disinterest and making it more important to ensure that their audience hygiene habits are strong.


On the plus side, the GMPT v2 interface is intended to include a **Compliance Dashboard** . That would allow senders to monitor domain alignment and other criteria that they may not have had visibility into before, making it easier to support improved deliverability to Gmail users.


### **Where to begin: Google Sender Requirements**


In 2024, Google[made an announcement](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/yahoo-and-gmails-2024-new-sending-requirements) and updated authentication requirements for bulk senders. These changes nudged senders to prioritize lower complaint rates, implement easier unsubscription approaches, and increased authentication.


**Requirement**


**Description**


Authentication


Senders are now required to implement Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and Domain Keys Identified Mail (DKIM) for mail to even be accepted. Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) is also required and, though there is no stated policy required, the implications are that a p=reject policy is swiftly becoming the standard as it affords recipients stronger protection.


One-click unsubscribe


Marketing mail must support a one-click unsubscribe mechanism (List-Unsubscribe header) to allow users to opt-out easily.


Complaint threshold


Senders should keep their spam complaint rate below 0.1% and must never exceed 0.3%.


## **How to get there: Strategies for optimal placement**


One of the first steps marketers should take to support a strong reputation with Google is to[warm their IPs](https://www.braze.com/resources/reports-and-guides/ip-warming) appropriately. But to continue that high performance, brands need to exercise diligence that extends long beyond the warming period—these efforts are continuous, and need to be treated that way to be successful. By taking small steps to prevent reputation issues, you can save yourself weeks or months of work that it takes to repair a reputation battered by bad decisions.


While there’s no one magic bullet that guarantees a higher reputation, the following factors play a key role and should be taken serious by anyone sending marketing emails:


### **1. Authenticate**


It doesn’t matter if you send millions of emails a day or only a few thousand; either way, it’s essential to declare who you are when sending mail to your customers. In email terms, this means establishing a send environment that is consistent, regular, and configured properly.


SPF and DKIM are standard operational procedures and serve to establish the authenticity of mail from the sender. DMARC is an attempt to take those measures further by informing providers how to react should they encounter unauthenticated mail. All of these measures are intended to ensure that mail from a sender’s domain(s) and IP(s) are properly attributed to them and that users don’t receive messages from an imposter (spoofer/phisher) that looks indistinguishable from the real brand.


### **2. Respect the audience**


This can seem like common sense—and, on a high level, of course, it is—but actually ensuring that this happens in connection with your email program can be a challenge. After all, even when a given individual gives your brand permission to email them, there’s often a lot that goes unsaid, leaving ambiguities that can complicate the sender/recipient relationship. For instance:


- How many times per day/week does the recipient want to hear from the sender?
- Is the content being sent relevant to their needs (both at the time they subscribe and then later on down the road)?
- Was the statement about what you’re offering in your email communications clear and transparent?
- Was permission to send the recipients asked for or just assumed because of some action that leads to a presumptive consent?
- Does the recipient even still want the mail they once asked for?


These factors (and more) are important for brands looking to establish an optimal reputation. Disconnects in a sender’s understanding of what their audience wants and needs can lead to complaints, messages marked as spam, or indifference—all of which are detractors from a sender’s reputation.


### **3. Utilize provider pools**


Compared to other inbox providers, Google provides perhaps the most robust provider generated feedback through its Postmaster Tools. These dashboards surface signals that senders should pay close attention to—for example, if a user-reported spam rating is high, the first check that marketers should make is to assess how their sending habits have deviated from sender best practices for bulk mailers. In general, being familiar with what those best practices are and then planning campaign strategy accordingly can help to prevent trouble down the road.


### **4. Warm up strategically**


A new domain and IP present opportunities for brands to establish a good reputation with inbox providers. However, internal or external pressure can sometimes lead to issues in connection with an IP warm-up. To see the best results, be sure to plan for a slow, gradual introduction of volume into Google's ecosystem. Tools like[Automated IP warming](https://www.braze.com/docs/user_guide/channels/email/email_setup/ip_warming/automated_ip_warming) can gradually ramp email volume from new dedicated IPs to build sender reputation with inbox providers. A sender who is too pushy and sends what they want without thinking about what their audience wants to receive will tend to face worse reputation outcomes than a sender who foregrounds the recipient experience and showcases to Google how much those individuals want to receive their messages. It's important for senders to prioritize active listening; when an inbox provider says, "I'm unsure" about a given email with a deferral response, the appropriate reaction is not to simply jam more mail through, it's to examine and assess why that action occurred and what you can do about it.


### **5. Consistency**


As a rule, senders who establish a consistent send cadence will tend to see a better reaction from Google. Bad actors in the email space have a tendency to inundate recipients with unwanted messages, and brands that accidentally mimic that behavior can see their sender reputation decline. If you're sending the bulk of your monthly emails on a single day, for instance, that's likely to trigger punitive measures from Google. It's not always possible to maintain a strict cadence—after all, sometimes you need to send out a big volume of emails all at once to meet a business need or satisfy a legal requirement—but the closer you can stick to that ideal, the better your outcomes will be.


### **6. Vigilance**


Reputation is not a “set it and forget it” proposition with Google. Maintaining a strong reputation relies on the reactions of email recipients—which means it’s vital for senders to stay attuned to the desires of their audiences and to adjust what they send based on the signals they receive. This focus should also extend to macro processes as well, with senders who ingest and react to Google’s feedback seeing better outcomes. What might that look like? For starters, that might include regular reviews of GPMT for domain and IP reputation changes, allowing senders to get ahead of issues before they manifest in placement problems.


### **7. Use all tools in the toolbox**


Mobile. Push. SMS. Social.[Digital marketing is an evolving landscape](https://www.braze.com/resources/reports-and-guides/the-cross-channel-marketing-difference-report) . New channels emerge and each application holds the promise of a user’s attention. The modern digital reality is that marketers utilizing only a single channel stand to miss potential conversions. For email marketers, these alternate channels represent a way to engage consumers across touchpoints. Providers’ algorithms or flagging interest may undermine optimal placement for your emails. A quick SMS, push, or other prompt draws attention to the email channel where providers rate desirability based on the recipient’s attention to the message.


## **Final thoughts**


At the end of the day, Google wants their users to get email that's of interest to them so that their subscribers are inclined to keep engaging with their services. By prioritizing technical sender requirements (authentication, one-click unsubscribe, etc.), brands can clear the initial hurdles. But to sustain a strong reputation and deliverability, marketers need to create email programs that consistently reward subscriber trust and respect their preferences (through relevant, desired, and predictable sending). With the right approach, getting into and staying relevant in a Google subscriber’s inbox is very possible.
